verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster. A psalm. Of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, a psalm: David's.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a heading, and in the Hebrew text it is verse 1 (the KJV prints it unnumbered, as 21:0). It tells the performers what to do: it is handed to the music leader, it is a mizmor (a song sung to strings or other accompaniment), and it is le-David. That last word is the reading the commentators fight over. The preposition lamed can mean 'of David' (by him), 'for David' (about him, or for his use) or 'belonging to the Davidic line'. Radak lists the options and points out that the psalm could be about David or about the king who comes from him; Malbim thinks the first two verses are a prologue before the story proper. The KJV 'A Psalm of David' takes the first option without saying that there is a choice. Cast the speaker as the congregation, not the king: the psalm talks to God about the king in the third person (v. 2 onward).

philological_notes.note: 'To the choirmaster', or 'for the leader'. The root can mean to excel or to supervise; in the psalm headings it names the official who has charge of the piece for the Temple liturgy. The meaning 'conductor' is a convention, since we have no other description of the office.
Lamed with a name: authorship, dedication or subject are all grammatically possible.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, in your strength the king rejoices, and in your deliverance how greatly he exults!
verses.translation_dramatic: LORD, the king is glad in your strength, and in your saving help, how he exults, how fiercely he exults!
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm opens by turning to God by name, and everything after that is addressed to him. The word order matters: 'LORD' comes first, before 'in your strength', so that the king is only an afterthought in his own song. The king's joy has a source outside himself. In the ancient Near East a king's strength was the thing his court was always proclaiming, and here it is explicitly God's. The two halves are the same thought in different words (Metzudat David says the second phrase just doubles the first), but the second adds a vowel of excitement: 'how greatly' (mah ... me'od) is an exclamation, not a question. The KJV 'shall joy ... shall he rejoice' puts the verbs in the future, 'shall', which the Hebrew does not require. The imperfect here is a general present: this is what the king does. The Hebrew also uses two different words for joy (samach and gil); the second is the louder, a whirling, shouting delight. The word for 'deliverance' is yeshu'ah, the root of the name Joshua and of Jesus (Yeshua). It means rescue in war or trouble, a concrete act, not the abstract 'salvation' that the KJV gives.

philological_notes.note: 'Your strength'. The word is pronounced with a short o (qamets chatuf), which Radak and Meiri note because it looks as if it should have a long a. Strength is something God gives (Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David), not the king's own.
The reading (Qere) is yagel; the written text (Ketiv) has a yod, yagil, as Radak points out, comparing the spelling of yagid in Eccl 10:20. The two forms are the same verb, to exult or spin with joy.
'In your deliverance'. Yeshu'ah is rescue in a concrete trouble, most often military. The same root appears again in v. 6.

verses.translation_literal: The desire of his heart you have given to him, and the request of his lips you have not withheld. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: What his heart longed for, you gave him. What his lips asked, you did not hold back. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: Two parallel halves, heart then lips: the thing wanted inwardly, and the thing said out loud. The point is that God answers both, including what the king never managed to say. Metzudat David says God gives what is wanted even where the king did not ask, and that all the more he will not refuse what the king asks aloud. The tense is a puzzle. The verbs are perfect ('you have given', 'you have not withheld'), and Radak and Metzudat David say that the prophets regularly speak of what will happen as if it had already happened, so that it could mean 'you will give'. The KJV, ASV and YLT read it as plain thanks for what has happened; say it as gratitude. The word 'areshet' (request) occurs only here in the Bible. Rashi says it means speech and has no parallel, and that Menachem brought a companion for it, rishyon, 'grant, permission', in Ezra 3:7 ('the grant of Cyrus king of Persia'); Ibn Ezra cites the same verse, and both, Rashi says, mean what the lips utter. Radak and Metzudat Zion likewise say it has no companion in Scripture. The KJV 'withholden' is an old participle; the Hebrew is a plain 'you did not hold back'. Selah closes the verse: a mark in the performance whose meaning has been lost. It is traditionally a pause, a lift of the voice or an instrumental interlude; do not play it as a word.

philological_notes.note: 'The request, the utterance'. A hapax legomenon, found only here in the Hebrew Bible. Rashi says it means speech and has no parallel, and reports that Menachem compared rishyon, 'grant, permission', in Ezra 3:7; Ibn Ezra makes the same comparison and says the aleph is an added letter, like the aleph of 'ezroa'. Both Rashi and Metzudat Zion gloss it as what the lips utter.
A liturgical mark of uncertain meaning, usually thought to call for a pause or a raised voice or instruments; the ancient translations do not agree about it.

verses.translation_literal: For you meet him with blessings of good; you set on his head a crown of pure gold.
verses.translation_dramatic: For you came out to meet him with blessings, all of them good, and you set on his head a crown of gold, refined and heavy.
verses.directors_commentary: The first image is of a host walking out of the city gate to meet a guest, before the guest has reached the door. The verb tekadd'menu comes from qedem, 'in front, before', so the blessings arrive ahead of the king, before he asks (Rashi, Meiri and Metzudat David all say before he asked). The KJV 'preventest' is the Latin sense of prevenire, 'to come before', and in modern English reads as the opposite: it means 'stop'. Read it as 'go out to meet'. 'Blessings of good' is a Hebrew way of saying every kind of good thing (Radak). The second half is the coronation. Paz is a term for gold that has been refined, and 'ateret is a ring-shaped crown, which the KJV simply calls a crown. A crown of that kind was a mark of rank and of victory in war. Rashi connects it with the crown of the king of Ammon placed on David's head (2 Samuel 12:30); Ibn Ezra imagines gems set around the gold. Note that God does the crowning, not a priest or a people.

philological_notes.note: 'You go out to meet him', literally 'you come in front of him'. The KJV 'preventest' preserves the Latin sense of coming before; in modern English it reads as the opposite.
Gold of the finest kind, refined; it is regularly set against ordinary gold (zahav) in poetry.

verses.translation_literal: Life he asked from you; you gave [it] to him: length of days, forever and ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: Life: that was what he asked of you. And you gave it to him, a length of days that does not end.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse begins with the single word 'life', the one thing the king asked for, placed at the front of the sentence for weight. This is the answer to the previous verse: the king's request was not for power or gold but for survival. The commentators ask when. Rashi hears David praying while he fled from Saul, and Malbim has the same moment; Radak takes it to be a long life in this world, and 'forever and ever' to be the world to come. The Hebrew is not that exact. 'Forever and ever' (olam wa'ed) is a stock phrase for a very long time, and in a royal setting it was part of the standard courtesy 'may the king live forever' (compare 1 Kings 1:31). The KJV text 'life of thee' is an old way to say 'from you'. Notice that 'life' (chayyim) is plural in Hebrew, as 'life' always is: Ibn Ezra puts it with other plural-only words like 'youth' (ne'urim). Do not play it as a claim of literal immortality; it is the language of the court and of hope for the dynasty.

philological_notes.note: 'Life'. Always plural in Hebrew; Ibn Ezra groups it with other plural-only nouns such as ne'urim (youth).

'Forever and ever', literally 'for the distant time and further'. In royal formulas it means 'for as long as can be imagined', not necessarily without end. Ibn Ezra says 'olam' can be as short as two generations.

verses.translation_literal: Great [is] his honor through your deliverance; splendor and majesty you lay upon him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Great is his glory, and it is your rescue that made it great. Splendor and majesty you lay upon him like a robe.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Honor' is kavod, which comes from the word for 'heavy': a man whose reputation weighs a lot. The point is the preposition. The king's glory is great 'in' or 'through' God's deliverance (bishu'atekha) and not in his own deeds; Radak says that when God rescues him from his enemies his honor grows in the eyes of the nations. 'Splendor and majesty' (hod wehadar) are the words used for the equipment of a king or of God himself (compare Psalm 96:6, 104:1), so the king is dressed in what belongs to heaven. The verb tashaweh, 'you lay, you set', means to place or to make level; Rashi and Ibn Ezra treat it as the same as 'tashit' in verse 4. The KJV 'honour and majesty hast thou laid upon him' is about right, but its 'salvation' misses that the deliverance here is a concrete victory, as in verse 2. Malbim goes further and hears 'shaveh' as 'equal': the glory fits him.

philological_notes.note: 'His honor, his glory'. From a root meaning 'to be heavy'; the weight is a person's standing.
'Splendor and majesty', a pair of words for the visible dignity of a king and of God; the same pair is said of God in the psalms.
'You lay, you place'. Rashi (citing Menachem) and Ibn Ezra treat it as the same as tashit in v. 4.

verses.translation_literal: For you make him blessings forever; you gladden him with gladness with your face.
verses.translation_dramatic: For you have made him a thing of blessing for all time, and made him glad, glad to the bone, in the light of your face.
verses.directors_commentary: Two surprises that the KJV flattens. First, 'you set him blessings': God does not just bless the king, he makes him into blessings, the way God told Abraham 'be a blessing' (Genesis 12:2), so that others will bless themselves by him (Radak cites Genesis 48:20, 'By you Israel will bless'). The KJV 'made him most blessed' turns a person who is a blessing into a person who receives one. Second, the sound play: techadehu bis'mchah, 'you make him rejoice with joy', joins a rare verb (chadah, 'to rejoice', as in 'Jethro rejoiced', Exodus 18:9) to the common word for joy. Radak says the second word is there to strengthen the first, as in Hebrew idioms like 'sacrificed a sacrifice'. The last words, 'et paneikha', 'with your face', are the high point of the verse: the king is glad because God turns his face toward him and is present. Radak says it is not his armies or silver that make him glad but the face of God. The KJV 'countenance' is stiff; say 'in your presence', and let the actor turn the face upward.

philological_notes.note: 'Blessings'. With the verb 'you set him', the sense is that he becomes a blessing, a person by whom others bless themselves, not only one who receives blessings.
'You make him rejoice'. A rare verb for joy, related to the one used of Jethro in Exodus 18:9. The following 'with joy' doubles it for emphasis.
'With your face, in your presence'. The face of God is the sign of his favor (compare the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:25); Radak reads it as God's turning toward him.

verses.translation_literal: For the king [is] trusting in YHWH, and in the loyal love of Most High he will not be shaken.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the king puts his trust in the LORD, and through the steadfast love of the Most High he will not be shaken.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the hinge of the psalm: the reason for everything said so far. Until now the speaker addressed God as 'you'; now the king is named as 'the king' and the voice steps back to explain why all this has happened. He trusts. The participle botea'ch is a standing condition, not a single act. Radak and Meiri say the point is that he does not trust in an army or in numbers. The second half uses two words. 'Chesed' is loyal love, the kind that comes from a promise or covenant: the KJV 'mercy' misses that it is a bond. 'Elyon', 'Most High', is an old name of God, and in an international setting it signals that the God who holds up this throne is above all other gods and their kings (Ibn Ezra says it is chosen to match the verb 'not shaken', since the one who is high is not moved). 'Bal yimmot', 'he will not totter', is the language of a building or a mountain; the king is imagined as a pillar that cannot be pushed over. Note that the KJV 'shall not be moved' here is correct.

philological_notes.note: Loyal love, faithfulness within a bond; stronger than the English 'mercy' of the KJV. Radak says everything God does for his creatures is chesed.
'Most High', here a name of YHWH. Ibn Ezra says it is chosen against the phrase 'will not be shaken': the one who is above is not moved.
'He will be shaken, he will totter'. The verb is used of foundations, mountains and feet that slip.

verses.translation_literal: Your hand will find all your enemies; your right hand will find those who hate you.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your hand will find them, every enemy you have. Your right hand will find them, all who hate you.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice now turns on the enemies, and the address is ambiguous. 'Your hand' may be addressed to God or to the king; Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra differ, and Radak even notes that the grammar of 'to all your enemies' versus 'those who hate you' is not parallel. Keep it ambiguous in the delivery, or lean on the king because the rest of the psalm is about him. The verb is the same twice, 'to find', and it is deliberately blunt: the hand does not strike but finds, as in a search from which nothing escapes. Meiri says the second use means literally that they will not be able to run away. Radak adds the sense 'be enough for' (cf. Numbers 11:22): the hand alone will suffice and no ally is needed. The KJV 'find out' suggests discovery of a secret; the Hebrew has no 'out'. The pairing 'enemies' and 'haters' is a standard doublet of ancient treaty and royal language, where the enemies of the king were also the enemies of his god. Hand and right hand: the right was the hand of strength and of oaths.

philological_notes.note: 'It will find'. A plain verb 'to find', which Radak and Metzudat David also read as 'suffice, be enough' (compare Numbers 11:22), while Meiri insists on 'find' in the second half: they cannot flee.
'Your right hand'. The hand of strength; in the psalms God's right hand is the instrument of rescue and of defeating the enemy.

verses.translation_literal: You will make them like a furnace of fire at the time of your face; YHWH in his anger will swallow them, and fire will consume them.
verses.translation_dramatic: You will make them like a blazing oven, in the hour when your face turns on them. The LORD in his anger will swallow them whole, and fire will eat them up.
verses.directors_commentary: The image is domestic, not epic: a tannur is the clay baking oven every household had, a beehive of fired clay stoked with brushwood until the walls glow. Radak and Meiri point out that the enemies are not the furnace that burns others, but the fuel inside it: they are the sticks in the oven. The KJV 'fiery oven' is right but loses this domesticity. 'At the time of your face' is a Hebrew idiom for the moment when God turns his face, which here means in anger; Rashi glosses it simply 'the time of your fury' and Radak and Meiri cite Lamentations 4:16, 'the face of the LORD has scattered them'. Compare the opposite use in v. 7, where God's face is a source of joy: the same face brings gladness to the king and fire to the enemies. The verbs then pile up: 'swallow' (bala', to gulp down) and 'consume' (akhal, to eat), with the final 'fire' held back to the end so that the verse closes on the word. The change from 'you' to 'YHWH' in the third person in the same verse is typical of Hebrew psalms and is not an error. Rashi calls the line a prayer, not a prediction.

philological_notes.note: 'At the time of your face', meaning when God turns his face in anger. Rashi glosses it 'the time of your fury'; Radak and Meiri compare Lamentations 4:16.
A clay baking oven; the enemies are the fuel in it, not its fire (Radak, Meiri).
'He will swallow them'. The verb of gulping something down whole; Meiri glosses it 'destroy'.

verses.translation_literal: Their fruit from the earth you will destroy, and their seed from the children of humankind.
verses.translation_dramatic: Their fruit you will root out of the earth, and their seed from among the sons of men.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a curse on a line of descent, in the language of farming. 'Fruit' (peri) and 'seed' (zera') are the same crop at two stages: the fruit is what has grown, the seed is what would have been planted next. Metzudat David says the second phrase just doubles the first, and both mean children. To ancient ears the worst fate was to have no descendants and so no one to keep one's name and perform the death rites; Radak and Meiri read it as 'no memory of them will remain'. 'Children of Adam' (bene adam) is simply the ordinary Hebrew phrase for people, not a reference to the first man, but it sets the king's enemies outside the human family. The KJV 'children of men' is accurate but sounds quaint, and the verb ta'abbed, from avad, is 'make perish', stronger than 'destroy' in modern English. The speaker is still addressing God or the king, and in Rashi's reading it is a prayer against Amalek.

philological_notes.note: 'Their fruit', meaning their offspring. The ending -mo is an archaic poetic form of 'their'. Metzudat David glosses it 'their children'.
'You will make perish'. The causative of avad, to be lost or die; much stronger than the mild English 'destroy'.

verses.translation_literal: For they have stretched out evil against you; they have planned a scheme; they will not succeed.
verses.translation_dramatic: For they reached out against you with evil. They devised a scheme, and they will not be able to carry it through.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse gives the reason for the fate of the enemies in the previous two verses: it is a crime, and it was plotted. 'They have stretched out' (natu) is the verb for stretching a tent, a hand or a net, so the image is a snare spread out, or a hand extended to seize; the KJV 'intended' loses the picture. The enemies' act is aimed at 'you', God or the king, and Meiri says that whoever fights David fights God, quoting Numbers 26:9. Radak says the punishment fits the plan: they plotted harm but could not carry it out. 'Mezimmah' is a plan, and in the Bible it can be a good plan or a wicked one; the KJV's 'mischievous device' and Webster's 'imagined' put the judgment in the noun, while the Hebrew only says 'a plan', and the evil comes from the context, 'against you'. The last two words 'bal yukhalu' are blunt and short, a single beat: 'they cannot'. The verb can mean 'be able' or 'prevail'. Metzudat David ties the line to Psalm 2: nations plot against the LORD and his anointed. Since psalm 21 is a royal psalm, the audience would have had that in the ear.

philological_notes.note: 'They stretched out'. The verb for stretching a tent, a hand or a net; used here with 'evil' as its object, as Ibn Ezra notes.
'A plan, a scheme'. In itself a neutral word that can mean careful thought; it is the context ('against you') that makes it wicked, which the KJV's 'mischievous' says outright.

verses.translation_literal: For you will set them [as] shoulder; with your bowstrings you will make ready [the arrow] against their faces.
verses.translation_dramatic: You will turn them, and all they will show you is a shoulder, a back running. Then the string is drawn taut, the arrow set, and what you aim at is no longer a back but their faces.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm has been praising the king's victories. Now it speaks to the LORD about the foe, in the second person, as in a battle speech. Two pictures stand side by side. First, the enemy is made 'shoulder': the Hebrew has only that one word, shekhem. I read it as the enemy made to turn the shoulder, to give his back and flee, which is what the KJV ('make them turn their back'), the ASV and the BBE do, and which matches Exodus 23:27, 'I will make all your enemies turn the back to you'. This is against the medieval commentators, who nearly all take shekhem as 'portion' or 'one': Rashi has God setting them aside as a portion whose goods Israel will divide as spoil (citing Isaiah 23:18); Ibn Ezra, noting the accent on the word, reads 'one shoulder', the enemies gathered together; Radak says God puts them all into one portion, so that they cannot mix with you and stand as one body facing you; Meiri has them as one portion before you; Metzudat David has them set apart in one corner as a target for the arrow; Metzudat Zion cites Genesis 48:22; Malbim ties it to the measuring lines of 2 Samuel 8:2. The Targum has 'one shoulder'. The poem works either way, and a director may let the actor hear both: a fleeing back, or a mass gathered as a single target.

Second, the archer. The verb tekhonen, 'make ready', has no object. Ibn Ezra and Radak say the arrows are understood, as in Psalm 11:2, 'they have made ready their arrow upon the string'. The KJV fills the gap, 'thine arrows upon thy strings', and the Hebrew is 'with' or 'by' your strings (a bet prefix), the bowstring doing the work. Note the grim irony on my reading: the fleeing enemy shows his back, yet the arrow is aimed at his face. For the actor, the shift from back to face is the turn of the verse: the enemy cannot escape, even by running. On the portion reading the shift is smaller: the massed foe stands in one place, and the arrows are aimed at the faces.

philological_notes.note: Primary sense is 'shoulder'; here the idiom is probably 'to make [someone give] the shoulder', that is, to put to flight (compare Ex 23:27), which is the reading of the KJV, ASV and BBE. The medieval commentators read it as 'portion, one band': Rashi (the share of spoil), Ibn Ezra (they are joined together), Radak ('one portion, all of them'), Meiri ('one portion before you'), Metzudat David (set apart on one side as a target), Metzudat Zion (compare 'one shekhem' in Gen 48:22). The Targum has 'one shoulder'.

From meitar, 'cord, string', here the bowstring (as in Ps 11:2 'upon the string', עַל יֶתֶר). Metzudat Zion glosses it the cord of the bow; Meiri notes that the 'strings' here stand for the arrows laid on them.
Polel of kun, 'be firm, set up, make ready'. Used of fitting the arrow to the string. The object is left out; Ibn Ezra and Radak call it a shortened expression, as the sense is clear.

verses.translation_literal: Be exalted, YHWH, in your strength; we will sing and we will make music [of] your might.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rise, O LORD, in the fullness of your strength! And we will sing, and we will strike the strings and sing again, of your might.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm that began with the king ends with the LORD, and the congregation speaks. The second verse of the psalm said, 'in your strength the king rejoices'; the last answers, 'be exalted, LORD, in your strength'. The same word, oz, opens and closes the poem, so the king's victory is shown to be God's. The cry is not a request for help but a request that God show himself, and a promise of song in return.

The KJV has 'so will we sing', which turns the second half into a result and flattens the grammar. The Hebrew has two cohortatives, 'let us sing, let us make music', a vow made by the people, with no 'so'. The two verbs also differ: shir is plain singing, zammer is song with instruments (the root of mizmor, the word translated 'psalm'), so the people promise voice and strings together. The KJV's 'praise' for zammer loses the music, and 'power' for gevurah is weaker than 'might', which in this psalm stands for the strength of a warrior. Rashi adds only that God is to rise over those who rise up against him; Radak spells out the point: all Israel will say, rise over the enemies in your strength, for the strength and the might are yours, not ours, and what we sing we sing because you gave it. Metzudat David reads it as a call that God rise up, in proportion to his great strength, to punish his enemies, and then we will sing. Stage it as a shout and then a hush, the people ready to sing.

philological_notes.note: Piel cohortative of zamar, 'make music, sing with an instrument'; the root of mizmor ('psalm'). Paired with nashirah ('let us sing'), it adds the instrument to the voice. KJV's 'praise' loses the musical sense.

'In your strength.' The same noun oz opens the psalm (v. 2, 'in your strength the king rejoices'), so the end of the poem answers the start; Ibn Ezra and Malbim make the same link. Radak says the people credit the strength to God, not to themselves.
